title: Algebraic Expressions and Identities
prerequisites: Basic idea of algebraic terms, coefficients, and like/unlike terms.
Comfort with the distributive property of multiplication over addition.
Linear equation and expression simplification skills from Chapter 2.

topics.title: Multiplication of Algebraic Expressions (Monomials, Binomials, Polynomials)
topics.quick_summary: Algebraic expressions are multiplied by applying the distributive law repeatedly, ensuring every term in one expression multiplies every term in the other.

detailed.definition: A monomial has one term, a binomial has two terms, and a polynomial has one or more terms. Multiplying expressions means applying the distributive property so each term of one expression multiplies each term of the other.
detailed.key_idea: When multiplying a binomial by a binomial, there are always FOUR term-to-term products (often remembered as FOIL: First, Outer, Inner, Last) before combining any like terms.
detailed.working_principle: Multiply monomial × monomial by multiplying coefficients and adding exponents of like variables; multiply monomial × polynomial by distributing across every term; multiply polynomial × polynomial by distributing every term of the first across every term of the second, then simplify by combining like terms.
applications: Calculating areas and volumes of geometric figures with algebraic (unknown) dimensions.
Expanding expressions as a preparatory step before factorisation or solving equations.

topics.real_life: Calculating the total area of a rectangular garden with algebraic side lengths (length = x+3, breadth = x+2) requires multiplying two binomials together.
points: Monomial × Monomial: multiply coefficients, add exponents of the same variable (xᵃ × xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ).
Distribute carefully: every term of the first expression must multiply every term of the second — none can be skipped.
Always combine like terms at the end to write the simplest final form of the product.
Keep track of signs carefully: a negative term multiplying a negative term gives a positive result.
mistakes: Forgetting to distribute a term across ALL terms of the other expression (missing cross-terms).
Adding exponents incorrectly, e.g., treating x² × x³ as x⁶ instead of the correct x⁵.
Sign errors when multiplying two negative terms or a positive and a negative term.
topics.memory_hook: 'FOIL for binomials: First, Outer, Inner, Last' — four products before you simplify.
topics.advanced: Multiplying polynomials is the algebraic version of the distributive law applied recursively — this same 'distribute every term across every term' logic scales up directly to multiplying matrices and polynomials with many terms in higher-level mathematics, so mastering it carefully now avoids much bigger headaches later.

topics.title: Standard Algebraic Identities
topics.quick_summary: Certain algebraic products follow fixed, memorable patterns called identities — (a+b)², (a−b)², and (a+b)(a−b) — which let you expand or factorise expressions instantly without repeating full multiplication.

detailed.definition: An algebraic identity is an equation that is true for ALL values of the variables involved (unlike an equation, which is true only for specific values); the three standard identities are (a+b)² = a²+2ab+b², (a−b)² = a²−2ab+b², and (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b².
detailed.key_idea: These identities are shortcuts derived once from direct multiplication — recognising when an expression MATCHES the pattern of a+b, a−b, or (a+b)(a−b) lets you skip full multiplication and write the answer directly.
detailed.working_principle: To apply an identity, identify which two terms play the role of 'a' and 'b' in the expression, then substitute directly into the matching identity formula rather than multiplying term by term.
applications: Fast mental arithmetic for squaring numbers close to round values (e.g., 98² using (100−2)²).
Simplifying and factorising algebraic expressions quickly in equations and further algebra topics.

topics.real_life: Mentally calculating 102² quickly as (100+2)² = 100² + 2×100×2 + 2² = 10404, without long multiplication, uses the (a+b)² identity directly.
points: (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b² — note the middle term is +2ab.
(a−b)² = a² − 2ab + b² — note the middle term is −2ab, but b² is still positive.
(a+b)(a−b) = a² − b² — the 'difference of squares' identity, with NO middle term.
These identities work with ANY values substituted for a and b, including negative numbers and other expressions.
mistakes: Forgetting the middle term entirely and writing (a+b)² = a² + b² (a very common error).
Using the wrong sign for the middle term in (a−b)², or wrongly making b² negative.
Misapplying (a+b)(a−b) = a²−b² to expressions that are not actually in the form (a+b)(a−b).
topics.memory_hook: 'Square of sum/difference: middle term never disappears' — a²+2ab+b² and a²−2ab+b² both keep the cross term.
topics.advanced: These three identities are the algebraic backbone of countless later results — from the Pythagorean-style expansions in coordinate geometry to the binomial theorem in higher classes, which generalises (a+b)² and (a+b)³ into (a+b)ⁿ for any power n.

formulas.name: Square of a Sum
formulas.variables: a, b = any two terms; one factor has a '+' and the other has a '−' between the same two terms.
formulas.when_to_use: Whenever multiplying a sum and a difference of the SAME two terms.
formulas.common_mistakes: Trying to apply this identity when the two binomials don't use the exact same a and b.
formulas.shortcut: Spot the pattern instantly: same two terms, opposite middle sign, product is just 'first² minus second²'.
